paras: The assault on Mingo Hamilton was an attack by a group of young men on Hamilton, a Black man, on the stoop of his home at 512 West Fifty-fifth Street in New York on the night of Saturday, September 19, 1903. Hamilton was struck with an ash can and cut or stabbed, and three days later Charles Kiernan was arrested and held in $500 bail on a charge of striking him. The two New York papers that covered the case disagreed over whether Hamilton's Black neighbors then fought Kiernan and his friends in a street riot.

According to the Evening World, four houses on the block between Tenth and Eleventh avenues were occupied only by Black tenants, whose arrival had "aroused the resentment" of white residents of long standing. The paper said fights between the two groups had been frequent and had lately involved knives.

Hamilton was sitting on his front stoop with a can of beer when, in the Evening World's words, "a crowd of young white men" came along and set upon him. That paper said they hit him on the head with an ash barrel, took what was left of his week's pay, drank his beer and cut him three times across the back with a razor. The Sun, which did not give the attackers' race, said one member of the gang struck him with an ash can and another stabbed him. Hamilton was treated at Roosevelt Hospital and came home on September 22.

That day Kiernan, of 420 West Forty-seventh Street, passed Hamilton's house and was recognized as one of the assailants. The Evening World reported that about fifty Black residents, with women bringing out knives and clubs, attacked Kiernan and five companions and left the white men "badly battered up." The Sun instead described an argument between Kiernan and a woman friend of Hamilton's, after which a janitress telephoned Police Headquarters that a race riot was in progress. Reserves from the West Forty-seventh Street station answered the call, and Detective O'Neill arrested Kiernan.

Kiernan was arrested on Hamilton's complaint, Hamilton swearing that he had been one of the gang. Arraigned the same afternoon in the West Side police court, he was held by Magistrate Deuel in $500 bail for examination. The Evening World added that no Black participants in the street fight were arrested and that several white women praised Kiernan and offered to testify for him. No report of the examination, a trial or any other arrest was found.

The case appeared in the Evening World on September 22 and The Sun on September 23, and no Black-press coverage of it was found. The Evening World headlined its story "Riot on West Side in War of Races," presented the street fight as Black "revenge," quoted Hamilton's neighbors in dialect and praised Kiernan's "bulldog courage," though it stated plainly that white men had robbed and cut Hamilton. The Sun, under the headline "Didn't Find a Race Riot," treated the episode as a false alarm and gave the assault on Hamilton two sentences.

reader.title: Assault on Mingo Hamilton
bases: A group of young men, white according to A1, set upon Hamilton on his stoop, struck him with an ash can or barrel and cut or stabbed him (A1, A2).

Two New York papers independently report that Hamilton was assaulted by a gang on Saturday night and that Kiernan was arrested for it (A1, A2); they disagree on the details of his wounds and on whether a street fight followed.

accounts.label: Evening World (same-day local report)
accounts.gist: A crowd of young white men beat, robbed and razor-cut Hamilton on his stoop; when Kiernan and five friends walked through the block on the day Hamilton came home from hospital, about fifty Black residents attacked them in 'revenge' until police reserves arrived.

accounts.label: The Sun (next-day report from police court)
accounts.gist: A gang assaulted Hamilton with an ash can and a knife; a friend of his recognized Kiernan and argued with him, a janitress called in a race riot, and the reserves found no riot but arrested Kiernan.

framing.detail: The Evening World headlined 'Riot on West Side in War of Races', framed the street fight as Black 'revenge', described Black residents as a 'black cloud' and quoted them in dialect, while calling Kiernan's fighting 'bulldog courage'; it also states plainly that white men attacked and robbed Hamilton.
The Sun headlined 'Didn't Find a Race Riot', treating the episode as a false alarm and the assault on Hamilton as a two-sentence police-court item without naming the attackers' race.

versions.value: A riot in which about fifty Black residents battered half a dozen white men

conflicts.note: A2 is a day later and drawn from the police-court arraignment; A1 is a same-day account with vivid unsourced detail. Neither is clearly better evidence; both agree reserves were called and Kiernan was arrested.

sources.note: Fullest account: crowd of young white men beat, robbed and razor-cut Hamilton on his stoop Saturday night; on his return from Roosevelt Hospital, about fifty Black residents fought Kiernan and five friends; Kiernan arrested on Hamilton's complaint.
